summary:
SIACHI: Sistema Ibérico de Alerta y Cartografía Histórica de Incendios (Iberian System of Warnings and Historical Cartography) is a web aplication that harmonizates the data from MODIS and VIIRS sensors (electromagnetic radiation), by classifying it by its resolution and power.

This app was necessary to unify these uncomparable data, making easier the action of comparing historical fires, see their advance or predict future performance. It is rather usefull specially for firefighters and forestry engineers, who dedicates to wildfire suppressions.

SIACHI is also a user-friendly web, easy to deal with for every person, with visual colour code, and an intuitive dashbord.

Moreover we added the function of 'warning confirmation' that allows citizens to 'ensure a fire' when data is not enough to do it due to its 'lack of confidence'. They would do it via Google Maps. Furthermore, we applicated a soil classification from SIGPAC to evaluate the hazard of each wildfire in relation to each type of ground.

In general, SIACHI is an interactive calendar designed to help professionals in the sector of wildfires to study, comprehend and predict how wildfires behave.
details:
SIACHI : Sistema Ibérico de Alerta y Cartografía Histórica de Incendios

 (Iberian System of Warnings and Historical Cartography).

Who We Are

We are a team of three Aerospace Engineering students from URJC in Spain united by a clear mission: bridging the gap between orbital remote sensing and operational wildfire management. While our academic background focuses on space systems, orbital physics, and Earth observation, our work in this project is designed directly for the forestry sector—supporting forestry engineers, environmental analysts, and wildfire suppression agencies with reliable, accessible intelligence derived from NASA satellite telemetry.

Why This Matters

Over the past decade, wildfires have escalated into an unprecedented environmental and civil emergency across Spain and the broader Iberian Peninsula. Between 2017 and 2026, wildfires burned approximately 1.54 million hectares across Spain alone, with 75% to 85% of that destruction concentrated in increasingly severe summer campaigns. Looking specifically at the three-year period from 2024 to 2026, fires across the Iberian Peninsula—a landmass of 583,254 km2 (58.33 million hectares or 144.13 million acres)—have scorched roughly 1.23 to 1.26 million hectares (3.05 to 3.12 million acres), representing over 2.1% of the entire peninsula lost in just three years. This surge has been driven by extreme summer megafires, including the 2022 season (marked by the Sierra de la Culebra disaster in Zamora), the historic August 2025 crisis—the worst summer of the 21st century in Spain, when nearly 393,000 hectares burned and massive smoke plumes across northwestern Iberia were captured by NASA’s Terra/MODIS satellite—and the severe July–August 2026 campaign, which claimed roughly 300,000 hectares.

To monitor and study emergencies of this scale, the forestry sector relies heavily on orbital data. NASA’s FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System) provides free global access to satellite thermal anomalies (hotspots), measuring brightness temperature in the mid- and thermal-infrared bands, Fire Radiative Power (FRP), and surface reflectance. However, raw FIRMS detections cannot be used directly in a simple way by forestry practitioners due to three fundamental limitations:

  1. Incompatible Satellite Sensors: NASA’s two primary fire-monitoring instruments—MODIS (aboard Terra and Aqua) and VIIRS (aboard Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21)—operate with different spatial resolutions and confidence metrics. MODIS offers the longest continuous historical archive (since 2000) at a ~1 km pixel resolution and reports detection confidence on a numeric 0–100 scale. Conversely, VIIRS provides a much sharper ~375 m resolution capable of detecting smaller fires (since 2012/2018) but expresses confidence categorically (low, nominal, and high).
  2. Fragmented Detections: A single thermal pixel detection does not constitute a wildfire. A large, multi-day forest fire generates thousands of disconnected detections across consecutive orbital passes, leaving analysts without a unified event structure.
  3. Disconnected Data Streams: NASA’s annual historical archives and its Near Real-Time (NRT) feeds (which retain only a rolling ~60-day window of provisional data) follow separate naming conventions and schemas that do not integrate seamlessly.

Our codebase, titled Harmonization MODIS and VIIRS, directly resolves these barriers so that both satellite constellations speak a single, consistent analytical language.

What We Built

We developed an end-to-end Wildfire Surveillance and Historical Intelligence Platform for the peninsula. The system ingests raw thermal anomalies from NASA satellites, filters out non-fire noise, harmonizes MODIS and VIIRS measurements, and aggregates individual pixel detections into named, trackable wildfire events spanning both real-time emergencies and a 25-year historical record.

Through a full-screen, interactive web user interface, forestry engineers and emergency planners can:

  • Monitor Active and Historical Wildfires: Explore a national map of the Iberian Peninsula governed by a clear visual color code that distinguishes active fires from closed events and categorizes individual detections by thermal intensity (low, medium, or high). At national zoom levels, fires appear as clean spatial markers; zooming in reveals the exact rectangular pixel footprints observed by each satellite pass.
  • Perform 10-Year Historical Benchmarks: By drawing a custom bounding box anywhere on the map, users can retrieve every wildfire recorded within that exact geographic area during the exact same calendar dates over the preceding decade. This enables analysts to immediately evaluate whether ongoing fire activity is anomalous or consistent with historical patterns for that specific region and season.
  • Inspect Comprehensive Fire Fact Sheets: Selecting any wildfire generates a structured analytical card displaying a dedicated minimap (perimeter envelope and constituent pixels), initial and final detection timestamps, minimum duration, peak FRP intensity, thermal footprint area, land-use breakdown, estimated consumed biomass, and multi-sensor confidence rating.

How It Works

The platform is engineered around a modular, four-stage architecture deployed via a single Docker command: an ETL Data Pipeline (backend/etls), a PostGIS Spatial Database (backend/databases), a REST API (backend/api), and a Web Map Frontend (frontend). All algorithmic thresholds, spatial buffers, and temporal windows are centralized in a single YAML configuration file (default.yaml), allowing forestry specialists to tune model sensitivity without modifying source code.

1. Multi-Source Ingestion and Digital Fingerprinting

The pipeline ingests and unifies two distinct data streams: NASA’s annual historical archives (from 2000 through the last completed calendar year) and daily Near Real-Time European feeds accessed via a secured NASA API token (automatically refreshing the latest 48 hours as satellite passes complete). The ingestion engine detects the instrument from file schemas rather than filenames, normalizes satellite identifiers, and computes a unique cryptographic fingerprint for every detection based on its physical attributes. This guarantees strict idempotency—re-processing files or overlapping historical and NRT feeds never creates duplicate records. Additionally, the system automatically calculates and flags any intra-year temporal gap between the end of the annual archive and the 60-day NRT window.

2. Spatial Cropping and Auditable Noise Filtering

Detections are spatially filtered to Spanish territory (the Iberian Peninsula, Balearic Islands, Canary Islands, Ceuta, and Melilla). Rather than silently discarding anomalous records, the pipeline flags invalid detections with explicit audit reasons so analysts can review every exclusion. Filtering removes non-vegetation heat sources labeled by NASA (industrial, marine, or volcanic), applies custom spatio-temporal exclusion zones (such as bounding boxes and dates isolating the 2021 La Palma eruption), and eliminates low-energy noise using sensor- and time-specific Fire Radiative Power (FRP) thresholds: 15 MW by day and 6 MW by night for VIIRS, compared to 30 MW by day and 12 MW by night for MODIS (accounting for MODIS’s larger pixel footprint and nocturnal ground cooling).

3. Pixel Projection and Cross-Sensor Harmonization

Valid detections are projected onto the terrain as physical pixel rectangles expanded by a 400-meter spatial buffer. Detections whose geometries intersect within the same daily time window are merged into a unified Observation. To reconcile the incompatible confidence scales of MODIS and VIIRS, we implemented a custom cross-sensor confidence matrix: observations detected by a single sensor family (even across two satellites of the same type, such as Terra and Aqua) are capped at Medium confidence, whereas achieving High or Very High confidence requires independent confirmation from both MODIS and VIIRS. Isolated, low-confidence single-sensor observations are excluded from forming fire events.

4. Spatiotemporal Event Clustering

To reconstruct the full lifecycle of a wildfire, the pipeline links consecutive daily observations located within 1 kilometer of one another into a single Wildfire Event. Each event is assigned a persistent identifier that remains stable across subsequent pipeline runs—if two initially separate fire fronts merge, the system retains the identifier of the older event and logs the merge. For every wildfire, the database tracks its bounding perimeter (envelope), temporal intensity curve, contributing sensors, and operational status, automatically transitioning an event from Active to Closed after 48 hours without new thermal detections.

5. Land-Use Enrichment, Biomass Estimation, and Scientific Transparency

Optionally, the pipeline cross-references detections with SIGPAC, Spain’s official 34 GB agricultural and forestry parcel registry across 50 provinces, classifying whether thermal activity occurred over forest land, pasture, or agricultural crops (helping distinguish agricultural stubble burns from forest wildfires). Furthermore, by integrating FRP across satellite passes and applying established physical conversion factors (~0.368 kg of dry biomass per megajoule), the pipeline estimates consumed vegetation in metric tons—a model validated against the June 2022 Sierra de la Culebra megafire, yielding approximately 100,000 tons of burned biomass.

Finally, to prevent misinterpretation by end users, the platform explicitly documents key remote-sensing caveats: thermal pixel footprints represent heat-detection areas rather than exact physical burn scars, observed durations represent minimum active windows between satellite overpasses, and NRT data remain provisional until superseded by NASA’s science-quality archive. Backed by automated unit and integration tests across every module, our working MVP is ready for deployment, with next steps focused on closing the intra-year NRT gap via direct FIRMS API queries, modeling orbital inclination in pixel geometries, and integrating an AI assistant over the structured Spanish fire summaries already generated by the pipeline.

Summing Up

Wildfires across Spain and the Iberian Peninsula have reached an unprecedented scale—claiming over 1.23 million hectares (more than 3 million acres) in the last three years alone—making timely, reliable Earth observation essential for modern forest management. By harmonizing NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS satellite constellations, our platform transforms fragmented, noisy thermal detections into structured, validated wildfire events spanning both real-time emergencies and a 25-year historical record.

As aerospace engineering students, our objective was never merely to process orbital telemetry, but to translate complex remote-sensing physics into an intuitive, scientifically transparent tool tailored to the operational realities of the forestry sector. Integrating cross-sensor confidence scoring, auditable noise filtering, SIGPAC land-use classification, biomass estimation, and 10-year historical benchmarking empowers forestry engineers and wildfire suppression teams to evaluate fire behavior in context and make faster, evidence-based decisions on the ground.

Built on a reproducible, containerized, and modular architecture, this working MVP establishes a solid foundation for next-generation wildfire intelligence. With upcoming enhancements—including direct FIRMS API gap-filling, orbital-inclination pixel modeling, and natural-language AI querying—the platform is engineered not only to help protect Iberian ecosystems today, but to scale seamlessly to any fire-prone region worldwide.
